lessons.title: What a name has to signal in five seconds
body: A product name is a compression of everything you worked out in Modules 1–6 — not a separate creative exercise. Its job is to help the intended customer understand or recognise the offer, ideally in five words or fewer, by communicating who it's for, what it helps achieve, or what kind of product it is.

Four ways a name can communicate
A descriptive name states plainly what the product is or does. An outcome-focused name leads with the result the customer wants. An audience-focused name leads with who it's for. A creative or abstract name is distinctive and memorable, but usually can't communicate the offer on its own. For a first digital product, clarity should generally beat cleverness — a confused customer doesn't buy, no matter how memorable the name is. A creative name can still work, as long as it's paired with a descriptive subtitle that does the explaining the name itself can't.

1. Outcome-focused names
These lead with the result: The 7-Day Content Planner, The Freelance Client System, The Beginner Fitness Blueprint. Useful when the outcome itself is the most compelling thing about the offer, and specific enough on its own to stand out.
2. Format-focused names
These lead with what the customer actually receives: Social Media Template Kit, Client Onboarding Toolkit, Weekly Study Planner. Useful when customers are uncertain what kind of thing they'd be buying — naming the format removes that uncertainty immediately.
3. Audience-focused names
These lead with who it's for: The Solo Creator Toolkit, The New Freelancer Guide, The Small Business Content System. Useful when naming the audience makes the offer feel instantly more relevant to the right person — and instantly less relevant to the wrong one, which is also useful.
4. Creative names with a descriptive subtitle
A distinctive brand name like ContentFlow can be memorable, but it doesn't communicate the offer by itself — which is why it needs a subtitle doing that work: “A practical weekly content planning system for small business owners.” Without the subtitle, a creative name is just a sound. These are hypothetical examples, not claims that any of these names are commercially available.

The five-word test
Hold every candidate against five questions: can the intended customer understand what the product is? Does the name communicate its audience, outcome or format? Is it specific enough to stand apart from a generic resource? Is it easy to pronounce and remember? Does it accurately represent what's actually included?
WEAK
“Ultimate Success.” — doesn't explain what the product is, who it serves, or what outcome it helps achieve.
STRONGER
“The Freelance Client Starter Kit.” — names the audience (freelancers), the stage (starting out with clients) and the format (a kit), all in five words.

Common naming mistakes
  • Sounds impressive, communicates nothing — if you can't say what it tells the customer, cut it.
  • Too broad — “Business Success Guide” could be anything; name the specific thing.
  • Promises results the product can't deliver — the name becomes a claim you'll have to defend.
  • Unnecessarily long — if it needs its own breath to say aloud, it's too long.
  • Unfamiliar jargon — a term your audience doesn't already use adds confusion, not clarity.
  • Confuses the format — a name that sounds like software when it's a PDF misleads before the sale even happens.
  • Imitates an existing brand too closely — beyond the confusion risk, this can create real legal exposure.

A workflow for naming your offer
  1. Revisit the target customer from Module 1.
  2. Revisit the main problem from Module 2.
  3. Revisit the outcome statement from Module 3.
  4. Review the core deliverable and bonuses from Module 4.
  5. Review your unique value proposition from Module 5.
  6. Review the price from Module 6.
  7. Identify the one thing the name should communicate most clearly — it usually can't communicate all six.
  8. Generate at least three name candidates.
  9. Evaluate each one against the five-word test above.
  10. Select the clearest candidate to carry into testing in Lesson 7.3.
Don't commit to the first name that comes to mind — it's rarely the clearest one, and you won't know that until you've generated a couple more to compare it against.

A worked example — hypothetical
Continuing the hypothetical small business owner from Modules 2–6: target audience is small business owners, the main problem is struggling to plan and create consistent social media content, the desired outcome is planning a week's content without starting from a blank page every day, and the core deliverable is a structured content planning system. Three candidates, three approaches:
  • The 7-Day Content Planner (outcome-focused) — clear and specific, but doesn't signal who it's for.
  • Small Business Content Toolkit (audience-focused) — instantly relevant to the right buyer, though a little generic on format.
  • ContentFlow: The Weekly Planning System (creative + descriptive subtitle) — memorable name, and the subtitle does the explaining.
For a first-time buyer who's never heard of this creator, Small Business Content Toolkit is probably the clearest of the three — it answers “is this for me” before the customer has to think about it, which matters more for a stranger than for someone who already trusts the brand. None of these three names are claimed to be available as real trademarks, domains or brands — that gets checked in Lesson 7.3.

Why comparison beats attachment
The first name you think of feels right mostly because it's the only one you've considered — not because you've tested it against anything. Once you draft two more and hold all three against the same five questions, you're choosing based on what actually communicates, rather than which option happened to arrive first and get attached to in your head.
lessons.insight: Draft three candidates before picking one — the first name you think of is rarely the clearest.

lessons.title: Position your offer clearly
body: Four words get used interchangeably here, and shouldn't be. Your product name identifies the product. Your product description lists what it contains. Your positioning statement explains who it's for, what problem it solves, what outcome it helps achieve, and why that matters to this specific customer. Your tagline is a short marketing expression — memorable, but not a substitute for actually explaining the offer. A catchy tagline with no positioning behind it is decoration on an empty box.

The four elements of a positioning statement
Target customer — who this is designed for, specifically. “Everyone” isn't a target customer; “small business owners who post on social media but have no content system” is. Main problem — the problem your customer actually experiences, straight from your Module 2 Problem Inventory, not a guess. Desired outcome — what they want to achieve, straight from your Module 3 Outcome Statement. Solution or differentiation — how your product actually helps, in terms of its approach, format, structure, practical resources, level of guidance or convenience. This can draw on the unique value proposition you defined in Module 5, but keep the two distinct: a positioning statement is one flowing sentence about the whole offer, while your UVP is its own separate statement of the specific meaningful difference. Don't invent a unique selling point the actual offer doesn't support — whatever you name here has to be something a customer would actually notice once they're using it.
VAGUE TARGET CUSTOMER
“People who want to grow their business.”
SPECIFIC TARGET CUSTOMER
“Small business owners who post on social media but have no system for deciding what to post.”

Turning this into a statement
A positioning statement reads naturally as: “For [target customer] who struggle with [main problem], [product name] is a [product type] that helps them [desired outcome] through [main method or distinctive feature].” The exercise below asks for the same four elements through a slightly shorter template — who, format, outcome and obstacle — that assembles into: “For [who], this offer is the [format] that [outcome] without [obstacle].” Who is your target customer. Format is your product type and differentiation together — what kind of thing it is and what makes it work. Outcome is the desired result. Obstacle is the main problem, framed as the thing the customer no longer has to deal with.

A worked example — hypothetical
Written in full: “For small business owners who struggle to plan consistent social media content, The 7-Day Content Planner is a practical planning toolkit that helps them organise a week's worth of posts through a structured planning workflow, editable templates and guided exercises.” Every part earns its place: the target customer is specific, not everyone; the problem is named plainly; the outcome is concrete; and the method names exactly what makes it work, not a vague claim of quality. Broken into the exercise's four fields: who — “small business owners who struggle to plan consistent social media content”; format — “practical content planning system”; outcome — “helps them organise a week's worth of posts”; obstacle — “starting from a blank page every time.” A weaker version — “This is a toolkit that helps people get better at social media” — is missing a specific audience, a specific problem, and a specific outcome; it could describe almost any social-media product that exists.

The same template, a different niche — hypothetical
A hypothetical fitness coach might fill the same four fields as: who — “beginners who want to work out at home but don't know where to start”; format — “guided 4-week workout program”; outcome — “helps them build a consistent exercise habit”; obstacle — “needing any equipment or gym membership.” Same structure, same discipline, completely different offer.

Communicating without exaggerating
Positioning should accurately reflect the product you actually built in Modules 1–6 — not a more impressive version of it. Avoid unsupported performance claims, guaranteed business growth, generic filler like “revolutionary” or “game-changing,” promises the product doesn't actually back up, and overly technical language that confuses the beginner you're trying to reach. If a sentence in your positioning statement wouldn't survive you explaining it honestly to the customer's face, it doesn't belong in it.
lessons.insight: A strong positioning statement should make it easy for the intended customer to recognise themselves, understand the problem being addressed and understand what the product helps them achieve.

lessons.title: Test and refine your positioning
body: You understand your product because you built it — every word of your name and positioning statement makes sense to you, because you already know what's behind it. A potential customer doesn't have that context. A name or sentence that reads perfectly clearly to you can still genuinely confuse someone meeting it for the first time, and you won't find that out by rereading it yourself one more time.

A simple clarity test
Show your candidate name and positioning statement to a few people who reasonably resemble your intended customer, and ask:
  1. What do you think this product helps someone do?
  2. Who do you think it's designed for?
  3. What do you think is included?
  4. Is anything confusing or unclear?
  5. What would you expect to receive after buying it?
If people consistently misunderstand what it is, who it's for, or what they'd get, the wording needs refining — not the product. A handful of informal conversations doesn't statistically validate your name or offer; it just surfaces confusion early enough to fix cheaply, before you've invested in branding or marketing around it.

The five-second test
Show just the name and your short positioning statement — no verbal explanation — and ask the person to describe what they think it is, in their own words. The goal isn't whether they like the name; it's whether they actually understood it. A name people enjoy but can't explain back to you has an attraction problem disguised as a branding success.

Comparing your candidates
Use the same criteria across all three candidates, rather than picking by personal taste: clarity, audience relevance, outcome relevance, memorability, accuracy, and ease of understanding. This isn't a validated scoring model — there's no formula that outputs a winner — it's a way to make sure you're comparing the same things about each candidate instead of comparing a feeling about one against a fact about another.

Basic availability checks
Before committing to a name commercially, check search engine results for it, relevant domain availability, social media handle availability, existing products using something similar, and relevant trademark databases for the markets you intend to sell in. A free domain or an open social handle does not mean the name is legally clear to use — those are convenience checks, not trademark clearance, and this lesson isn't performing a legal trademark search for you. Where commercial or trademark risk is meaningful, get qualified legal advice before you commit.
lessons.insight: The purpose of testing is to discover confusion before investing in branding, design and marketing.

exercise.instructions: Draft three name candidates, then complete the positioning statement template.

prompts.title: Naming Prompt
prompts.purpose: Use this to generate and stress-test name candidates.
prompts.template: You are a positioning and naming specialist. My offer: {{m4.coreDeliverable}}. My target customer and their desired outcome: {{m1.topMarket}} / {{m3.outcomeStatement}}. Give me 8 candidate names for this offer, drawing on at least three different naming approaches — outcome-focused, format-focused, audience-focused, and (if you include a creative or abstract name) paired with a short descriptive subtitle. Each name must make clear, in 5 words or fewer, who it's for or what format it is (not a vague or clever name with no information in it), and label which approach each one uses. Then pick your top 3 and explain in one sentence each why they'd stand out in a $27 digital-product marketplace. Don't claim or imply that any candidate is available as a domain, trademark or social handle — that has to be checked separately. If my offer description or target customer above doesn't give you enough to name it precisely, tell me what's missing and ask before generating names. If any name candidate only works because of an assumption about how my customer talks or what they already know, flag that assumption alongside the name.

prompts.title: Positioning Statement Prompt
prompts.purpose: Use this to draft a clear positioning statement using the who/format/outcome/obstacle template.
prompts.template: You are a positioning consultant using DigitalOps's positioning template — for [who], this offer is the [format] that [outcome] without [obstacle]. My target customer: {{m1.topMarket}}. My problem inventory: {{m2.summary}}. My desired outcome: {{m3.outcomeStatement}}. My offer: {{m4.summary}}. My unique value proposition: {{m5.uvpStatement}}. My strongest name candidate so far: {{m7.topName}}. Draft three positioning statement options using exactly that structure — for [who], this offer is the [format] that [outcome] without [obstacle] — each phrasing the same facts slightly differently so I can compare them. Use my unique value proposition only as context for what's genuinely distinctive about the offer — the positioning statement itself must stay in the who/format/outcome/obstacle structure above, not restate the UVP as its own sentence. Keep every option grounded in what I've actually told you — don't invent a differentiator, feature or claim about the offer that I haven't described. If any of the inputs above is missing or too thin to draft a credible statement, tell me what's missing and ask before drafting anything. After the three options, flag any wording that sounds exaggerated or unsupported rather than something this specific offer can actually back up.
